packs.title: At the Café Table
packs.description: Common drinks, utensils, and breakfast staples for cafés, kitchens, and shared tables.

words.meaningMnemonic: At a café, a <reading>COP–POOH</reading> duo steals every cup: the cop grabs it and Pooh drinks it dry. Their p sounds collide as the empty <vocabulary>drinking glass</vocabulary> rolls across the table. コップ usually means a handleless glass or cup; a mug is more specifically マグカップ.

contextSentences.ja: 水をコップに入れてください。
contextSentences.en: Please pour water into the glass.

contextSentences.ja: 新しいコップを二つ買った。
contextSentences.en: I bought two new cups.

words.meaningMnemonic: A giant <reading>fork</reading> stabs the café table and lifts the whole meal into the air. Everyone must cling to its four prongs until the <vocabulary>fork</vocabulary> puts lunch back down. フォーク is the ordinary table utensil; the familiar English word is stretched into the Japanese loan sound.

contextSentences.ja: パスタはフォークで食べます。
contextSentences.en: I eat pasta with a fork.

contextSentences.ja: フォークをもう一本お願いします。
contextSentences.en: One more fork, please.

words.meaningMnemonic: A silver <reading>spoon</reading> grows long enough to scoop up the moon, then drops it into your soup. The shining crescent floating in the bowl makes this impossible <vocabulary>spoon</vocabulary> unforgettable. スプーン is the ordinary eating utensil, often marked with で when it is what you use.

contextSentences.ja: スープをスプーンで飲んだ。
contextSentences.en: I ate the soup with a spoon.

contextSentences.ja: 小さいスプーンで砂糖を混ぜる。
contextSentences.en: I stir the sugar with a small spoon.

words.meaningMnemonic: A runaway <reading>knife</reading> slices your sandwich, plate, and table neatly in two before you can catch it. You lock the overenthusiastic <vocabulary>knife</vocabulary> in the cutlery drawer. ナイフ usually means a small or table knife; 包丁 is the usual word for a kitchen knife.

contextSentences.ja: このナイフはよく切れる。
contextSentences.en: This knife cuts well.

contextSentences.ja: 子ども用のナイフを用意した。
contextSentences.en: I set out a children's knife.

words.meaningMnemonic: You open a bottle of <reading>cola</reading>, and a dark fizzy geyser launches you through the ceiling. When you land, the room is sticky with <vocabulary>cola</vocabulary>. コーラ means the soft drink, and its middle vowel is held long in Japanese.

contextSentences.ja: 氷なしのコーラをください。
contextSentences.en: A cola without ice, please.

contextSentences.ja: コーラを二人で分けた。
contextSentences.en: The two of us shared a cola.

words.meaningMnemonic: A carton of <reading>milk</reading> sprouts arms and milks the café's coffee machine until every cup turns white. The customers chase the carton down to get their <vocabulary>milk</vocabulary> back. ミルク is common for milk as a drink or café addition; 牛乳 is the everyday native term for cow's milk.

contextSentences.ja: コーヒーにミルクを少し入れる。
contextSentences.en: I put a little milk in my coffee.

contextSentences.ja: 温かいミルクを飲んで寝た。
contextSentences.en: I drank warm milk and went to bed.

words.meaningMnemonic: A wheel of <reading>cheese</reading> melts itself into a yellow slide across your toast. You ride the gooey <vocabulary>cheese</vocabulary> straight onto the breakfast plate. チーズ is the ordinary loanword for cheese, with its long vowel clearly held.

contextSentences.ja: パンにチーズをのせて焼いた。
contextSentences.en: I put cheese on bread and toasted it.

contextSentences.ja: このチーズは香りが強い。
contextSentences.en: This cheese has a strong aroma.

words.meaningMnemonic: A block of <reading>butter</reading> puts on skates and races around the hot pan. It melts before the finish line, leaving the whole pan coated in <vocabulary>butter</vocabulary>. バター is the everyday food word, and the final vowel is long in Japanese.

contextSentences.ja: フライパンにバターを入れた。
contextSentences.en: I put butter in the frying pan.

contextSentences.ja: バターをぬったパンが好きです。
contextSentences.en: I like bread spread with butter.

words.meaningMnemonic: A tub of <reading>yogurt</reading> erupts like a cold white volcano when you peel back the lid. The tangy flood buries your spoon, so you must eat your way through the <vocabulary>yogurt</vocabulary> to rescue it. ヨーグルト is the ordinary cultured dairy food, not a yogurt-flavored drink unless the context says so.

contextSentences.ja: 毎朝ヨーグルトを食べています。
contextSentences.en: I eat yogurt every morning.

contextSentences.ja: ヨーグルトにバナナを入れた。
contextSentences.en: I added banana to the yogurt.

words.meaningMnemonic: Your <reading>toast</reading> pops out wearing a tiny crown and demands that breakfast salute it. When nobody bows, the offended slice burns itself darker, becoming unmistakable <vocabulary>toast</vocabulary>. トースト usually means sliced bread browned in a toaster, and the first vowel is long.

contextSentences.ja: 朝はトーストと卵を食べます。
contextSentences.en: I eat toast and an egg in the morning.

contextSentences.ja: トーストが少し焦げてしまった。
contextSentences.en: The toast got a little burnt.

contextSentences.ja: パンを二枚トーストしてください。
contextSentences.en: Please toast two slices of bread.

words.meaningMnemonic: A marching band tries to <reading>jam</reading> through the mouth of a fruit jar and gets stuck. They squeeze the berries into a sweet purple <vocabulary>jam</vocabulary> that spills over the toast. ジャム is fruit spread; the same word can also describe a musical jam in the right context.

contextSentences.ja: いちごのジャムを作りました。
contextSentences.en: I made strawberry jam.

contextSentences.ja: トーストにジャムをぬる。
contextSentences.en: I spread jam on the toast.

words.meaningMnemonic: A runaway <reading>café</reading> sprouts wheels and serves coffee while racing down the street. You catch the mobile <vocabulary>café</vocabulary> only by grabbing its enormous espresso cup. カフェ is a modern café or coffee shop; 喫茶店 often suggests a more traditional coffee shop.

contextSentences.ja: 駅前のカフェで待ち合わせよう。
contextSentences.en: Let's meet at the café in front of the station.

contextSentences.ja: このカフェは朝七時に開く。
contextSentences.en: This café opens at seven in the morning.

packs.title: Casual Meals & Treats
packs.description: Popular menu items, snacks, and everyday foods found at restaurants, shops, and home.

words.meaningMnemonic: A towering <reading>hamburger</reading> grows legs and runs away with the bun still clamped around it. You catch the escaped <vocabulary>burger</vocabulary> by following its trail of pickles. ハンバーガー means the bun sandwich; the long final sound helps distinguish it from ハンバーグ.

contextSentences.ja: 昼にハンバーガーを食べた。
contextSentences.en: I ate a hamburger for lunch.

contextSentences.ja: このハンバーガーは野菜が多い。
contextSentences.en: This burger has lots of vegetables.

words.readingMap: ハ・ン・バ・ー・ガ・ー

words.meaningMnemonic: A cook shouts <reading>Hamburg!</reading> and kicks away both halves of the bun before serving the meat patty on a plate. The banished buns make it clear this is <vocabulary>Hamburg steak</vocabulary>, not a burger. ハンバーグ is the Japanese-style ground-meat patty served without a bun; ハンバーガー is the sandwich.

contextSentences.ja: 晩ご飯にハンバーグを作った。
contextSentences.en: I made Hamburg steak for dinner.

contextSentences.ja: ハンバーグにソースをかける。
contextSentences.en: I pour sauce over the Hamburg steak.

words.meaningMnemonic: A chef cuts <reading>OMELET + RICE</reading> down to two labels, オム and ライス, then wraps the rice in the omelet like a yellow blanket. The snug bundle becomes <vocabulary>omurice</vocabulary>. オムライス is the Japanese dish of seasoned rice with omelet, not plain omelet and rice served separately.

contextSentences.ja: この店のオムライスは卵がふわふわだ。
contextSentences.en: The omelet on this restaurant's omurice is fluffy.

contextSentences.ja: 子どもにオムライスを作った。
contextSentences.en: I made omurice for the child.

words.meaningMnemonic: A potato hears <reading>fried potato</reading> and jumps whole into the fryer, but the cook yanks it out and cuts it into crisp strips. What lands on your plate is a pile of <vocabulary>French fries</vocabulary>. フライドポテト means fries or chips in Japanese, not any potato that happens to be fried.

contextSentences.ja: フライドポテトをみんなで分けた。
contextSentences.en: We all shared the French fries.

contextSentences.ja: このフライドポテトは塩が少ない。
contextSentences.en: These fries don't have much salt.

words.readingMap: フ・ラ・イ・ド・ポ・テ・ト

words.meaningMnemonic: Choco, a chocolate bar, is late to its own birthday party and melts while running through the door. Everyone points and cries, <reading>CHOCO—LATE!</reading>, then scoops the melted <vocabulary>chocolate</vocabulary> onto the cake. チョコレート is the full word; チョコ is its common casual shortening.

contextSentences.ja: 妹にチョコレートをあげた。
contextSentences.en: I gave my younger sister some chocolate.

contextSentences.ja: このケーキにはチョコレートが入っている。
contextSentences.en: This cake contains chocolate.

words.readingMap: チョ・コ・レ・ー・ト

words.meaningMnemonic: A <reading>cookie</reading> thief tiptoes into the kitchen, but each stolen biscuit crunches like thunder. The crumbs expose both the thief and every missing <vocabulary>cookie</vocabulary>. クッキー covers cookies and sweet biscuits; the stop in the middle is crisp and the last vowel is long.

contextSentences.ja: 午後のおやつにクッキーを食べた。
contextSentences.en: I ate cookies for my afternoon snack.

contextSentences.ja: 友達とクッキーを焼きました。
contextSentences.en: I baked cookies with a friend.

words.meaningMnemonic: A giant <reading>doughnut</reading> rolls out of the bakery and traps you in its sugary center. You eat through the ring-shaped <vocabulary>doughnut</vocabulary> to escape. ドーナツ is the everyday loanword for a doughnut, whether ring-shaped or filled.

contextSentences.ja: 駅でドーナツを三つ買った。
contextSentences.en: I bought three doughnuts at the station.

contextSentences.ja: このドーナツは中にクリームが入っている。
contextSentences.en: This doughnut has cream inside.

words.meaningMnemonic: Your <reading>cereal</reading> flakes assemble into a tiny army and paddle across the milk. You stop the breakfast invasion by eating every piece of <vocabulary>cereal</vocabulary>. シリアル most often means breakfast cereal; context can also give it the broader sense of serial or serialized.

contextSentences.ja: 忙しい朝はシリアルを食べます。
contextSentences.en: On busy mornings, I eat cereal.

contextSentences.ja: シリアルに冷たいミルクをかけた。
contextSentences.en: I poured cold milk over the cereal.

words.meaningMnemonic: A bottle of <reading>mayonnaise</reading> paints every dish white, including your dessert and your shoes. You wrestle away the creamy <vocabulary>mayo</vocabulary> before it reaches the coffee. マヨネーズ is the full word; マヨ is the common casual shortening.

contextSentences.ja: サラダにマヨネーズを少しかける。
contextSentences.en: I put a little mayonnaise on the salad.

contextSentences.ja: マヨネーズは別にしてください。
contextSentences.en: Please put the mayonnaise on the side.

words.meaningMnemonic: A bottle of <reading>ketchup</reading> tries to catch up with your fries, squirting a red trail as it runs. It finally tackles the plate and covers every chip in <vocabulary>ketchup</vocabulary>. ケチャップ is the tomato condiment; the middle consonant closes sharply before プ.

contextSentences.ja: オムライスにケチャップで絵を描いた。
contextSentences.en: I drew a picture in ketchup on the omurice.

contextSentences.ja: ケチャップをもう少しください。
contextSentences.en: Please give me a little more ketchup.

words.meaningMnemonic: A restaurant's <reading>lunch</reading> bell launches your coworkers out of their chairs and into a midday buffet. The last person there loses the final <vocabulary>lunch set</vocabulary> to a hungry pigeon. ランチ can mean lunch generally or a restaurant's special midday set, depending on context.

contextSentences.ja: 同僚とランチに行きました。
contextSentences.en: I went to lunch with a coworker.

contextSentences.ja: 今日のランチは魚の料理です。
contextSentences.en: Today's lunch set is a fish dish.

words.meaningMnemonic: At a <reading>barbecue</reading>, the grill grows legs and chases every guest until they feed it a skewer. Once satisfied, it cooks an enormous <vocabulary>BBQ</vocabulary> feast for everyone. バーベキュー can name either the cooking event or the grilled food, and both long vowels are audible.

contextSentences.ja: 週末に庭でバーベキューをします。
contextSentences.en: We're having a barbecue in the garden this weekend.

contextSentences.ja: バーベキュー用の野菜を切った。
contextSentences.en: I cut vegetables for the barbecue.

words.readingMap: バ・ー・ベ・キュ・ー

words.meaningMnemonic: You gasp <reading>OOH, DON!</reading> as Don pulls one noodle from his bowl and it stretches across the entire room. The thick, chewy rope can only be <vocabulary>udon</vocabulary>. うどん names the wheat noodles or a dish made with them; the cue is approximate but keeps both Japanese chunks in order.

contextSentences.ja: 寒い日は温かいうどんが食べたい。
contextSentences.en: On cold days, I want to eat hot udon.

contextSentences.ja: この店はうどんの量が多い。
contextSentences.en: This restaurant serves large portions of udon.

words.meaningMnemonic: A <reading>TACO–YAH–KEY</reading> lands on a round griddle, yells YAH, and uses a key to flip balls filled with octopus. The three-part commotion produces a tray of piping-hot <vocabulary>takoyaki</vocabulary>. たこやき is the Osaka-style octopus snack, not a taco; the English chunks are a close sound path through た・こ・や・き.

contextSentences.ja: 祭りで熱いたこやきを食べた。
contextSentences.en: I ate hot takoyaki at the festival.

contextSentences.ja: たこやきを六個注文した。
contextSentences.en: I ordered six pieces of takoyaki.

packs.title: Conversation Signals
packs.description: Short, high-frequency reactions and transitions that make everyday spoken Japanese feel responsive and natural.

words.meaningMnemonic: A magician opens an empty hat and snaps <reading>AH!</reading> when he remembers the rabbit is still at home. That sharp discovery bursts out as <vocabulary>oh!</vocabulary> before he can explain. あっ marks a sudden realization or reaction; the tiny っ cuts it off abruptly.

contextSentences.ja: あっ、財布を家に忘れた。
contextSentences.en: Oh, I left my wallet at home.

contextSentences.ja: あっ、バスが来たよ。
contextSentences.en: Oh, the bus is here.

words.meaningMnemonic: A fish answers your phone, and you jerk back with <reading>EH?!</reading> before dropping it in surprise. Your startled <vocabulary>huh?</vocabulary> is the only response the fish gets. えっ expresses surprise or disbelief and is sharper than a neutral request to repeat something.

contextSentences.ja: えっ、今日は休みなの？
contextSentences.en: Huh? We have today off?

contextSentences.ja: えっ、もう十時？
contextSentences.en: Huh, is it already ten?

words.meaningMnemonic: A gatekeeper checks your name twice—<reading>EH, EH</reading>—then stamps both forms and waves you through. The two approving nods mean <vocabulary>yes</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>that's right</vocabulary>. ええ is a conversational affirmative; はい is generally safer in very formal situations.

contextSentences.ja: ええ、その案で大丈夫です。
contextSentences.en: Yes, that plan is fine.

contextSentences.ja: ええ、私も参加します。
contextSentences.en: Yes, I'll join too.

words.meaningMnemonic: <reading>MA-AH</reading>, the mother llama stretches both arms between two fighting alpacas. Her long calming sound turns the quarrel into <vocabulary>well...</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>now, now</vocabulary> instead of a brawl. まあ can soften surprise, hesitation, resignation, or an attempt to calm someone.

contextSentences.ja: まあ、焦らずに考えよう。
contextSentences.en: Well, let's think without rushing.

contextSentences.ja: まあまあ、そんなに怒らないで。
contextSentences.en: Now, now, don't get so angry.

words.meaningMnemonic: A wall of dishes topples toward you and your mouth jumps through <reading>OOH–WAH!</reading> as they smash. The crash pulls out an instinctive <vocabulary>whoa!</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>yikes!</vocabulary>. うわ reacts to something shocking, awful, or impressively overwhelming, depending on tone.

contextSentences.ja: うわ、雨が急に強くなった。
contextSentences.en: Whoa, the rain suddenly got heavy.

contextSentences.ja: うわ、この箱は重い！
contextSentences.en: Yikes, this box is heavy!

words.meaningMnemonic: The gift box opens and a tiny sun rises out of it while everyone cries <reading>WA-AH!</reading>. Its warm light turns the reaction into delighted <vocabulary>wow!</vocabulary> rather than alarm. わあ usually expresses wonder, delight, or happy surprise, with the final sound held open.

contextSentences.ja: わあ、海がきれい！
contextSentences.en: Wow, the sea is beautiful!

contextSentences.ja: わあ、プレゼントをありがとう。
contextSentences.en: Wow, thank you for the present.

words.meaningMnemonic: A hen lays a square egg, and the farmer leans closer with <reading>HEH-EH?</reading> instead of running away. His raised eyebrow asks <vocabulary>oh, really?</vocabulary> as he inspects every corner. へえ shows interested surprise or curiosity; intonation can make it warmer or more skeptical.

contextSentences.ja: へえ、そんな方法があるんだ。
contextSentences.en: Oh, really? There's a way to do that?

contextSentences.ja: へえ、この店は百年も続いているの？
contextSentences.en: Really, has this shop been open for a hundred years?

words.meaningMnemonic: Two yo-yos have climbed a mountain for days, chanting <reading>EE-YO, EE-YO</reading> with every step. They reach the summit just as the sun rises—<vocabulary>at last</vocabulary>, the moment is <vocabulary>finally</vocabulary> here. いよいよ points to the long-awaited or decisive stage now arriving.

contextSentences.ja: いよいよ明日が本番だ。
contextSentences.en: Tomorrow is finally the big day.

contextSentences.ja: いよいよ新しい店が開く。
contextSentences.en: The new shop is finally opening.

words.meaningMnemonic: A runner drags two enormous <reading>TOE–TOE</reading> feet across the finish line. After a painfully long race, both toes cross <vocabulary>finally</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>in the end</vocabulary>. とうとう stresses the eventual outcome of a long process, whether that result is welcome or not.

contextSentences.ja: とうとうこの本を読み終えた。
contextSentences.en: I finally finished reading this book.

contextSentences.ja: 雨はとうとう夜までやまなかった。
contextSentences.en: In the end, the rain didn't stop until night.

words.meaningMnemonic: At dawn, a dancer in a zoot suit plants one toe on a piano key and refuses to lift it. The audience chants <reading>ZOOT—TOE!</reading> as the same note sounds <vocabulary>the whole time</vocabulary> and remains <vocabulary>by far</vocabulary> the longest note in the show. ずっと can mark continuous duration or emphasize a much greater degree.

contextSentences.ja: 駅でずっと友達を待っていた。
contextSentences.en: I waited for my friend at the station the whole time.

contextSentences.ja: こちらの道のほうがずっと近い。
contextSentences.en: This route is much closer.

words.meaningMnemonic: <reading>NAN–TOE–KAH</reading>: Nan kicks a jammed car door with her toe, startling a crow into shouting KAH. The door flies open, so she escapes <vocabulary>somehow</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>one way or another</vocabulary>. なんとか means managing despite difficulty; it can also introduce an unspecified something in other constructions.

contextSentences.ja: 締め切りまでになんとか終わった。
contextSentences.en: I managed to finish by the deadline.

contextSentences.ja: 時間がないので、そこをなんとかお願いします。
contextSentences.en: We're out of time, so please find some way to make it work.

packs.title: Clear, Careful & Complete
packs.description: Everyday adverbs for describing how well, how clearly, or how completely something happens.

words.meaningMnemonic: Sticky <reading>SAP–PARRY</reading> splashes a fencer, so she parries it with a blast from a garden hose. The wash leaves her completely <vocabulary>refreshed</vocabulary>. Asked whether any sap remains, she answers, “<vocabulary>not at all</vocabulary>.” さっぱり can mean feeling clean or refreshed, while さっぱり＋negative means not at all.

contextSentences.ja: シャワーを浴びてさっぱりした。
contextSentences.en: I took a shower and felt refreshed.

contextSentences.ja: この説明はさっぱり分からない。
contextSentences.en: I don't understand this explanation at all.

words.meaningMnemonic: An earthquake lifts a palace, but a sheikh catches it and carries it across the desert without dropping one tile. The crowd chants <reading>SHEIKH—CARRY!</reading> as he holds it <vocabulary>firmly</vocabulary> and works <vocabulary>dependably</vocabulary>. しっかり describes firm action, proper preparation, or a reliable person.

contextSentences.ja: 手すりをしっかり持ってください。
contextSentences.en: Please hold the handrail firmly.

contextSentences.ja: 明日の準備をしっかりしておこう。
contextSentences.en: Let's prepare properly for tomorrow.

contextSentences.ja: 彼は若いけれど、考え方がしっかりしている。
contextSentences.en: He is young, but he has a level-headed way of thinking.

words.meaningMnemonic: A gymnast balances a <reading>KEY–CHIN–TOE</reading> tower: a key on her chin and a teacup on her toe. Nothing is crooked because she arranged every piece <vocabulary>properly</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>neatly</vocabulary>. きちんと emphasizes correct, orderly, or well-groomed execution.

contextSentences.ja: 使った道具はきちんと戻してください。
contextSentences.en: Please put the tools back properly after using them.

contextSentences.ja: 彼はいつもきちんとした服を着ている。
contextSentences.en: He always wears neat clothes.

words.meaningMnemonic: A tailor falls into a <reading>PIT–TALLY</reading> and tallies every measurement before climbing out. The suit he makes fits <vocabulary>exactly</vocabulary> and is a <vocabulary>perfect fit</vocabulary>. ぴったり is used for sizes, timing, matches, or amounts that fit exactly.

contextSentences.ja: この靴は足にぴったりだ。
contextSentences.en: These shoes fit my feet perfectly.

contextSentences.ja: 電車は九時ぴったりに着いた。
contextSentences.en: The train arrived at exactly nine.

words.meaningMnemonic: A <reading>BAT–CHEERY</reading> photographer flaps into the studio and makes every grumpy subject smile. Not one shot needs fixing; the photos come out <vocabulary>perfectly</vocabulary>, completely <vocabulary>spot on</vocabulary>. ばっちり is casual and upbeat, often describing preparation, appearance, or a result that turned out just right.

contextSentences.ja: 旅行の準備はばっちりです。
contextSentences.en: We're perfectly prepared for the trip.

contextSentences.ja: その答えでばっちりだよ。
contextSentences.en: That answer is spot on.

words.meaningMnemonic: <reading>NAN–DA–KAH</reading>: Nan opens a box, hears a duck mutter DA and a crow answer KAH, but sees nothing inside. The room feels <vocabulary>somehow</vocabulary>, just <vocabulary>a little</vocabulary>, strange. なんだか introduces a vague feeling or impression whose reason the speaker cannot quite name.

contextSentences.ja: 今日はなんだか静かですね。
contextSentences.en: It feels strangely quiet today.

contextSentences.ja: なんだか甘い物が食べたい。
contextSentences.en: For some reason, I feel like eating something sweet.

words.meaningMnemonic: An <reading>ICKY NARI</reading> monster bursts from a clean teapot and covers Nari in green slime. With no bubbling or warning first, it happens <vocabulary>suddenly</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>without warning</vocabulary>. いきなり emphasizes the missing lead-in, often more strongly than merely saying something happened quickly.

contextSentences.ja: いきなり電話が切れた。
contextSentences.en: The call suddenly disconnected.

contextSentences.ja: 彼はいきなり立ち上がった。
contextSentences.en: He stood up without warning.

words.meaningMnemonic: Zoe crosses a desert just to return one borrowed vase. At the door she holds up the shattered pieces and gasps, <reading>WAS A—WAS A</reading> whole vase before that needless trip; it is a spectacular case of <vocabulary>going out of one's way</vocabulary> for you. わざわざ highlights intentional extra effort, with gratitude or irritation depending on context.

contextSentences.ja: わざわざ駅まで迎えに来てくれた。
contextSentences.en: They went out of their way to meet me at the station.

contextSentences.ja: お忙しい中、わざわざありがとうございます。
contextSentences.en: Thank you for making the effort despite being busy.

words.meaningMnemonic: <reading>GUS–SURREY</reading> sleeps in a Surrey carriage while an elephant lands on its roof and crushes the bed flat. Gus does not twitch because he is sleeping <vocabulary>soundly</vocabulary>, completely <vocabulary>fast asleep</vocabulary>. ぐっすり most often modifies sleeping and suggests deep, satisfying sleep.

contextSentences.ja: 昨夜はぐっすり眠れた。
contextSentences.en: I slept soundly last night.

contextSentences.ja: 赤ちゃんは今ぐっすり寝ている。
contextSentences.en: The baby is fast asleep now.

words.meaningMnemonic: A spy in a costume with only COS left on its torn label bumps a guard and whispers SORRY while sliding behind him. <reading>COS(tume)—SORRY</reading> puts him inside the vault <vocabulary>secretly</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>stealthily</vocabulary> before the guard notices. こっそり describes doing something quietly so other people will not notice.

contextSentences.ja: 妹はこっそりケーキを食べた。
contextSentences.en: My younger sister secretly ate the cake.

contextSentences.ja: 猫がこっそり部屋に入ってきた。
contextSentences.en: The cat crept stealthily into the room.

words.meaningMnemonic: A hacker named <reading>HACK–KIRI</reading> slices every patch of fog off the computer screen. The hidden answer now appears <vocabulary>clearly</vocabulary> for everyone to see. はっきり applies to clear sights, sounds, memories, statements, or firm decisions.

contextSentences.ja: もう少しはっきり話してください。
contextSentences.en: Please speak a little more clearly.

contextSentences.ja: 山の形がはっきり見える。
contextSentences.en: I can see the shape of the mountain distinctly.

words.meaningMnemonic: A giant sock grows arms and carries every object out of a castle, right down to the last spoon. The king yells <reading>SOCK—CARRY!</reading> as the k sounds collide and the rooms become <vocabulary>completely</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>entirely</vocabulary> empty. すっかり marks a change or action that has reached its full extent.

contextSentences.ja: 外はすっかり暗くなった。
contextSentences.en: It has become completely dark outside.

contextSentences.ja: 約束をすっかり忘れていた。
contextSentences.en: I had completely forgotten the promise.

words.meaningMnemonic: A <reading>TAP–PULLEY</reading> turns the tap and hauls up bucket after bucket until a river overflows the room. There is <vocabulary>plenty</vocabulary> of water, filled <vocabulary>fully</vocabulary> and then some. たっぷり means an ample amount and can modify quantities, time, or doing something thoroughly.

contextSentences.ja: 野菜をたっぷり入れてください。
contextSentences.en: Please add plenty of vegetables.

contextSentences.ja: 週末はたっぷり休みました。
contextSentences.en: I got plenty of rest over the weekend.

packs.title: Home Comfort
packs.description: Furniture, rooms, and household basics used throughout an ordinary day at home.

words.meaningMnemonic: A dining <reading>table</reading> grows to the ceiling and carries your breakfast beyond reach. You climb its legs to recover every plate from the giant <vocabulary>table</vocabulary>. テーブル is a table used for dining, work, or display; 机 is more specifically a desk.

contextSentences.ja: 料理をテーブルに並べた。
contextSentences.en: I arranged the food on the table.

contextSentences.ja: このテーブルは四人用です。
contextSentences.en: This table is for four people.

words.meaningMnemonic: A hungry <reading>sofa</reading> swallows everyone who sits down, then burps out their shoes. You rescue the family by stuffing the <vocabulary>couch</vocabulary> with cushions until it sneezes. ソファ is the ordinary padded seat for two or more people.

contextSentences.ja: ソファに座って本を読んだ。
contextSentences.en: I sat on the sofa and read a book.

contextSentences.ja: 猫がソファで寝ている。
contextSentences.en: The cat is sleeping on the couch.

words.meaningMnemonic: Your <reading>bed</reading> sprouts wheels and races away just as you are about to sleep. You tackle the runaway <vocabulary>bed</vocabulary> and chain it to the bedroom wall. ベッド means the sleeping furniture; the clipped consonant and final vowel are part of its Japanese loan form.

contextSentences.ja: 疲れたので早くベッドに入った。
contextSentences.en: I was tired, so I went to bed early.

contextSentences.ja: ベッドの下に靴がある。
contextSentences.en: There are shoes under the bed.

words.meaningMnemonic: The <reading>shower</reading> sprays upward instead of down and pins you to the bathroom ceiling. You turn off the impossible <vocabulary>shower</vocabulary> only after the whole room is soaked. シャワー is the shower itself or taking one, with a long final vowel.

contextSentences.ja: 運動の後でシャワーを浴びた。
contextSentences.en: I took a shower after exercising.

contextSentences.ja: この部屋にはシャワーがあります。
contextSentences.en: This room has a shower.

words.meaningMnemonic: In a chaotic kitchen, the chef balances an entire cooking <reading>KIT–CHIN</reading> on his chin. When the pots tumble into the soup, nobody can mistake the room for anything but a <vocabulary>kitchen</vocabulary>. キッチン is the modern kitchen or cooking area; 台所 is the native Japanese alternative.

contextSentences.ja: 父はキッチンで夕食を作っている。
contextSentences.en: My father is making dinner in the kitchen.

contextSentences.ja: 新しいキッチンは明るくて広い。
contextSentences.en: The new kitchen is bright and spacious.

words.meaningMnemonic: A <reading>veranda</reading> detaches from the apartment and sails through the sky with all the laundry still hanging. You steer the flying <vocabulary>balcony</vocabulary> home by pulling on a bedsheet. ベランダ is the exterior platform of a house or apartment, even when English speakers would call it a balcony.

contextSentences.ja: ベランダに洗濯物を干した。
contextSentences.en: I hung the laundry on the balcony.

contextSentences.ja: ベランダから山が見える。
contextSentences.en: You can see the mountain from the balcony.

words.meaningMnemonic: The <reading>curtain</reading> wakes up, grabs the sunrise, and yanks it back outside so you can keep sleeping. That heroic pair of <vocabulary>curtains</vocabulary> leaves the bedroom dark. カーテン refers to window curtains or drapes, with the first vowel held long.

contextSentences.ja: 朝になったのでカーテンを開けた。
contextSentences.en: Morning came, so I opened the curtains.

contextSentences.ja: 青いカーテンを選びました。
contextSentences.en: I chose blue curtains.

words.meaningMnemonic: A springy <reading>cushion</reading> launches you from the sofa and catches you again before you hit the floor. You strap down the rebellious <vocabulary>cushion</vocabulary> before sitting a second time. クッション is a loose padded cushion; it can also mean cushioning or shock absorption.

contextSentences.ja: 腰の後ろにクッションを置いた。
contextSentences.en: I put a cushion behind my lower back.

contextSentences.ja: このクッションはとても柔らかい。
contextSentences.en: This cushion is very soft.

words.meaningMnemonic: A thirsty <reading>towel</reading> drinks the entire swimming pool while you dry your hands. The swollen <vocabulary>towel</vocabulary> then floods the bathroom when you wring it out. タオル is the ordinary cloth for drying hands, dishes, hair, or the body.

contextSentences.ja: 手を洗ってタオルで拭いた。
contextSentences.en: I washed my hands and dried them with a towel.

contextSentences.ja: 旅行にはタオルを二枚持って行く。
contextSentences.en: I'll take two towels on the trip.

words.meaningMnemonic: Tish arrives wearing a <reading>TISH–SHOE</reading> made from hundreds of tissues. Rain dissolves the shoe, leaving one soggy <vocabulary>tissue</vocabulary> stuck to every toe. ティッシュ usually means facial tissue or tissue paper, not biological tissue.

contextSentences.ja: ティッシュを一枚取ってください。
contextSentences.en: Please take one tissue.

contextSentences.ja: かばんにティッシュを入れてある。
contextSentences.en: I keep tissues in my bag.

words.meaningMnemonic: A pair of <reading>pajamas</reading> yawns, climbs into your bed, and falls asleep before you can put it on. You must wake the sleepy <vocabulary>pajamas</vocabulary> before bedtime. パジャマ is sleepwear, usually treated as one clothing category rather than a grammatical plural.

contextSentences.ja: お風呂の後でパジャマに着替えた。
contextSentences.en: I changed into pajamas after my bath.

contextSentences.ja: 冬用の暖かいパジャマを買った。
contextSentences.en: I bought warm pajamas for winter.

words.meaningMnemonic: Two <reading>slippers</reading> skate across the hallway and tackle anyone who enters wearing outdoor shoes. Once they catch you, the indoor <vocabulary>slippers</vocabulary> refuse to leave your feet. スリッパ usually means backless indoor footwear, including guest slippers, rather than soft bedroom shoes only.

contextSentences.ja: 玄関でスリッパに履き替えた。
contextSentences.en: I changed into slippers at the entrance.

contextSentences.ja: お客様用のスリッパを出した。
contextSentences.en: I put out slippers for the guest.

words.meaningMnemonic: A bag shouts <reading>GO, ME!</reading> and volunteers to be the first thing thrown into the truck. The collectors obey and carry away all the <vocabulary>trash</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>garbage</vocabulary> with it. ゴミ is the everyday word for rubbish; local sorting rules often add a category before it.

contextSentences.ja: ゴミは朝八時までに出してください。
contextSentences.en: Please put out the garbage by eight in the morning.

contextSentences.ja: 公園でゴミを拾った。
contextSentences.en: I picked up trash in the park.

packs.title: Everyday Clothes
packs.description: Core clothing and accessory words for getting dressed, shopping, and describing what people wear.

words.meaningMnemonic: A rack of <reading>shirts</reading> grows arms and buttons itself around every shopper who walks past. You escape the clingy <vocabulary>shirt</vocabulary> by undoing its sleeves. シャツ is a general shirt; compounds such as Tシャツ and ワイシャツ identify particular styles.

contextSentences.ja: 白いシャツに着替えた。
contextSentences.en: I changed into a white shirt.

contextSentences.ja: このシャツは洗濯しやすい。
contextSentences.en: This shirt is easy to wash.

words.meaningMnemonic: A wool sweater climbs onto a stage and orders the crowd to <reading>SAY—TAR!</reading>. Every shout makes it knit another wall until the enormous <vocabulary>sweater</vocabulary> covers the house. セーター is a knitted sweater or jumper; both ー marks are long vowels.

contextSentences.ja: 寒いのでセーターを着た。
contextSentences.en: It was cold, so I put on a sweater.

contextSentences.ja: 母が赤いセーターを編んでくれた。
contextSentences.en: My mother knitted me a red sweater.

words.meaningMnemonic: Your <reading>coat</reading> wraps itself around a snowman and refuses to come home. You trade the snowman a scarf to recover the warm <vocabulary>coat</vocabulary>. コート usually means an overcoat; in sports contexts the same sound can mean a court.

contextSentences.ja: 外に出る前にコートを着た。
contextSentences.en: I put on my coat before going outside.

contextSentences.ja: 黒いコートを椅子に掛けた。
contextSentences.en: I hung the black coat on the chair.

words.meaningMnemonic: A <reading>jacket</reading> zips itself shut around a lamp and marches out as a glowing person. You catch the runaway <vocabulary>jacket</vocabulary> by pulling its sleeves. ジャケット is a short outer garment or suit jacket; heavier long outerwear is usually コート.

contextSentences.ja: 会議ではジャケットを着ます。
contextSentences.en: I wear a jacket at meetings.

contextSentences.ja: このジャケットには内側にもポケットがある。
contextSentences.en: This jacket has a pocket on the inside too.

words.meaningMnemonic: A zoo elephant hides a huge bone in each trouser leg, then tries to walk away stiff-legged. The keeper shouts <reading>ZOO—BONE!</reading> as the animal's <vocabulary>pants</vocabulary> clatter across the floor. ズボン is the ordinary Japanese word for trousers or pants; ZOO—BONE is a close sound cue, with BONE supplying the final nasal.

contextSentences.ja: このズボンは少し長い。
contextSentences.en: These trousers are a little long.

contextSentences.ja: 仕事用のズボンを買った。
contextSentences.en: I bought trousers for work.

words.meaningMnemonic: A spinning <reading>skirt</reading> becomes a helicopter and lifts its wearer over the school gate. When it lands, the dizzy <vocabulary>skirt</vocabulary> is twisted around backward. スカート is the waist garment, with a long middle vowel; the same sound can mean a protective machine panel in technical contexts.

contextSentences.ja: 姉は青いスカートを選んだ。
contextSentences.en: My older sister chose a blue skirt.

contextSentences.ja: このスカートにはポケットがある。
contextSentences.en: This skirt has pockets.

words.meaningMnemonic: A formal <reading>suit</reading> interviews its own wearer and rejects him for being underdressed. He wins the job only after the matching <vocabulary>suit</vocabulary> approves his tie. スーツ normally means a matching business or formal outfit, not any clothes that happen to suit someone.

contextSentences.ja: 面接には紺色のスーツで行った。
contextSentences.en: I went to the interview in a navy suit.

contextSentences.ja: 新しいスーツを自分のサイズに直してもらった。
contextSentences.en: I had my new suit altered to fit me.

words.meaningMnemonic: A <reading>necktie</reading> tightens like a lasso and drags its owner into an important meeting. The boss loosens the formal <vocabulary>tie</vocabulary> before it strangles the presentation. ネクタイ is the clothing item, not the verb to tie something.

contextSentences.ja: 父は毎朝ネクタイを結ぶ。
contextSentences.en: My father ties a necktie every morning.

contextSentences.ja: そのシャツにはこのネクタイが合う。
contextSentences.en: This tie goes well with that shirt.

words.meaningMnemonic: A champion <reading>belt</reading> wraps around your waist and rings a boxing bell whenever your trousers slip. The noisy <vocabulary>belt</vocabulary> keeps them up but ruins every quiet room. ベルト can be a clothing belt, safety belt, or machine belt depending on context.

contextSentences.ja: ズボンに茶色いベルトを合わせた。
contextSentences.en: I matched a brown belt with the trousers.

contextSentences.ja: 食べすぎたので、ベルトを少しゆるめた。
contextSentences.en: I ate too much, so I loosened my belt a little.

words.meaningMnemonic: Your <reading>pocket</reading> opens a secret door and swallows your keys, phone, and finally your whole arm. You sew shut the greedy <vocabulary>pocket</vocabulary> before it eats your wallet too. ポケット is a pocket in clothing, a bag, or similar object.

contextSentences.ja: 鍵をコートのポケットに入れた。
contextSentences.en: I put the key in my coat pocket.

contextSentences.ja: ポケットから小銭が落ちた。
contextSentences.en: Some coins fell out of my pocket.

words.meaningMnemonic: A sailor named <reading>BO–TAN</reading> tans beneath a giant button that switches the sun on. When he presses the glowing <vocabulary>button</vocabulary>, every lamp on the boat ignites too. ボタン can be a clothing fastener or a control you press; context tells which.

contextSentences.ja: シャツのボタンが一つ取れた。
contextSentences.en: One button came off my shirt.

contextSentences.ja: 青いボタンを押してください。
contextSentences.en: Please press the blue button.

words.meaningMnemonic: A pair of <reading>sneakers</reading> sneaks out at midnight and leaves muddy footprints through the house. You catch the guilty <vocabulary>trainers</vocabulary> hiding under the bed. スニーカー means casual athletic shoes; the long vowels reflect the Japanese loan form.

contextSentences.ja: 散歩には軽いスニーカーを履く。
contextSentences.en: I wear light sneakers for walks.

contextSentences.ja: 白いスニーカーをきれいに洗った。
contextSentences.en: I washed my white sneakers thoroughly.

packs.title: Travel & Places
packs.description: Transport, accommodation, and navigation words for moving through a city or taking a trip.

words.meaningMnemonic: A delivery <reading>truck</reading> grows monster tires and carries an entire supermarket down the road. Every shelf stays inside the enormous <vocabulary>lorry</vocabulary> until it reaches your house. トラック is the goods vehicle; in sports, トラック can also mean a running track.

contextSentences.ja: 大きなトラックが荷物を運んでいる。
contextSentences.en: A large truck is carrying cargo.

contextSentences.ja: 店の前に配送のトラックが止まった。
contextSentences.en: A delivery truck stopped in front of the shop.

words.meaningMnemonic: An <reading>elevator</reading> refuses to stop at the roof and lifts its passengers into the clouds. They parachute back while the runaway <vocabulary>lift</vocabulary> keeps climbing. エレベーター is the enclosed machine between floors; an open moving staircase is an エスカレーター.

contextSentences.ja: エレベーターで十階まで上がった。
contextSentences.en: I took the elevator up to the tenth floor.

contextSentences.ja: このエレベーターは点検中です。
contextSentences.en: This elevator is being inspected.

words.readingMap: エ・レ・ベ・ー・タ・ー

words.meaningMnemonic: An <reading>escalator</reading> grows faster with every step until shoppers shoot onto the next floor like rockets. A guard pulls the plug on the wild <vocabulary>escalator</vocabulary>. エスカレーター is the moving staircase, with two long vowels in its Japanese loan form.

contextSentences.ja: エスカレーターでは手すりにつかまってください。
contextSentences.en: Please hold the handrail while riding the escalator.

contextSentences.ja: 次の階へはエスカレーターで行けます。
contextSentences.en: You can take the escalator to the next floor.

words.readingMap: エ・ス・カ・レ・ー・タ・ー

words.meaningMnemonic: A hotel <reading>lobby</reading> holds an election and every sofa campaigns for the best waiting spot. Guests must vote before they can sit in the <vocabulary>lounge</vocabulary>. ロビー is the shared entrance or waiting area of a hotel, theater, or large building.

contextSentences.ja: ホテルのロビーで友達を待った。
contextSentences.en: I waited for my friend in the hotel lobby.

contextSentences.ja: ロビーには無料の新聞がある。
contextSentences.en: There are free newspapers in the lobby.

words.meaningMnemonic: A huge sign marked <reading>FRONT</reading> falls off the hotel and lands squarely on the check-in counter. The receptionist works beneath it, making that counter the <vocabulary>front desk</vocabulary>. In a hotel, フロント means reception or the front desk, not simply the front side of anything.

contextSentences.ja: 鍵をフロントに返してください。
contextSentences.en: Please return the key to the front desk.

contextSentences.ja: フロントで近くの地図をもらった。
contextSentences.en: I got a local map at reception.

words.meaningMnemonic: Your <reading>passport</reading> sprouts wings at immigration and tries to cross the border without you. The officer catches the flying <vocabulary>passport</vocabulary> and stamps it before returning it. パスポート is the official travel document, with both long vowels held in Japanese.

contextSentences.ja: 空港でパスポートを見せた。
contextSentences.en: I showed my passport at the airport.

contextSentences.ja: 旅行の前にパスポートの期限を確認した。
contextSentences.en: I checked my passport's expiration date before the trip.

words.meaningMnemonic: A wheeled <reading>suitcase</reading> packs its owner, zips itself shut, and rolls toward the airport. You rescue the trapped traveler by tackling the runaway <vocabulary>suitcase</vocabulary>. スーツケース is the travel case; スーツ alone means a formal suit.

contextSentences.ja: 服をスーツケースに詰めた。
contextSentences.en: I packed my clothes into the suitcase.

contextSentences.ja: 赤いスーツケースを預けました。
contextSentences.en: I checked the red suitcase.

words.readingMap: ス・ー・ツ・ケ・ー・ス

words.meaningMnemonic: A giant pair of scissors cuts リュックサック in half, and the surviving <reading>RÜCK</reading> half straps itself onto your shoulders. The shortened word still carries everything like a <vocabulary>backpack</vocabulary>. リュック is the common clipping of リュックサック, from German Rucksack; it means a backpack or rucksack.

contextSentences.ja: 水と地図をリュックに入れた。
contextSentences.en: I put water and a map in my backpack.

contextSentences.ja: このリュックは軽くて丈夫だ。
contextSentences.en: This backpack is light and sturdy.

words.meaningMnemonic: At the hire counter, scissors snip the ル out of <reading>RENTA(L) CAR</reading> before handing you the keys. The shortened sign now labels your temporary <vocabulary>rental car</vocabulary>. レンタカー is clipped from レンタルカー and can refer to the hired car or the car-rental service.

contextSentences.ja: 空港でレンタカーを借りた。
contextSentences.en: I rented a car at the airport.

contextSentences.ja: レンタカーは明日の朝返します。
contextSentences.en: I'll return the rental car tomorrow morning.

words.meaningMnemonic: Your <reading>drive</reading> takes a strange turn when the car rejects work and heads for the beach by itself. The unplanned seaside <vocabulary>car trip</vocabulary> lasts all afternoon. ドライブ often means a drive for travel or pleasure; operating a vehicle as a skill is 運転.

contextSentences.ja: 日曜日に海までドライブした。
contextSentences.en: We went for a drive to the coast on Sunday.

contextSentences.ja: 天気がいいからドライブに行こう。
contextSentences.en: The weather is nice, so let's go for a drive.

words.meaningMnemonic: A pump pours <reading>gasoline</reading> into a thirsty car, which gulps until its fuel gauge bursts through the roof. The overfed engine sprays <vocabulary>petrol</vocabulary> from its exhaust. ガソリン is vehicle fuel; a filling station is commonly a ガソリンスタンド.

contextSentences.ja: 出発前にガソリンを入れた。
contextSentences.en: I filled up with gasoline before leaving.

contextSentences.ja: この車はあまりガソリンを使わない。
contextSentences.en: This car doesn't use much gasoline.

packs.title: Digital Essentials
packs.description: Everyday device and internet vocabulary for work, study, communication, and troubleshooting.

words.meaningMnemonic: A digital <reading>tablet</reading> mistakes itself for medicine and jumps into a giant's glass of water. The soaked <vocabulary>tablet computer</vocabulary> keeps displaying apps from the bottom. タブレット can mean a tablet computer or a pill-like tablet, so context matters.

contextSentences.ja: タブレットで電子書籍を読んだ。
contextSentences.en: I read an e-book on a tablet.

contextSentences.ja: 会議ではタブレットでメモを取る。
contextSentences.en: I take notes on a tablet during meetings.

words.meaningMnemonic: A paper <reading>NOTE + PASOCON</reading> folds around a tiny personal computer and snaps shut like a clamshell. When it opens again, the notebook has become a portable <vocabulary>laptop</vocabulary>. ノートパソコン literally combines ノート with the clipped パソコン, and specifically means a notebook computer.

contextSentences.ja: ノートパソコンをカフェに持って行った。
contextSentences.en: I took my laptop to the café.

contextSentences.ja: このノートパソコンは電池が長く持つ。
contextSentences.en: This laptop's battery lasts a long time.

words.readingMap: ノ・ー・ト・パ・ソ・コ・ン

words.meaningMnemonic: A computer <reading>keyboard</reading> replaces every key with a tiny doorbell. Typing one email rings the entire neighborhood, so you cover the noisy <vocabulary>keyboard</vocabulary>. キーボード is a computer or musical keyboard; context identifies which.

contextSentences.ja: 新しいキーボードは音が静かだ。
contextSentences.en: The new keyboard is quiet.

contextSentences.ja: キーボードで名前を入力してください。
contextSentences.en: Please enter your name using the keyboard.

words.meaningMnemonic: A real <reading>mouse</reading> grabs the computer pointer and drags it across the screen with its tail. You click the squeaking <vocabulary>computer mouse</vocabulary> and it demands cheese. マウス can mean the computer device or an actual mouse in some names and compounds; ネズミ is the usual animal word.

contextSentences.ja: マウスで画像を選びます。
contextSentences.en: I select the image with the mouse.

contextSentences.ja: このマウスは右手でも左手でも使える。
contextSentences.en: This mouse can be used with either hand.

words.meaningMnemonic: Your <reading>monitor</reading> grows eyes and monitors you back whenever you look at the screen. You turn the nosy <vocabulary>display</vocabulary> toward the wall, but it swivels around. モニター can mean a display, a monitoring device, or a tester depending on context.

contextSentences.ja: 大きなモニターで動画を確認した。
contextSentences.en: I checked the video on a large monitor.

contextSentences.ja: モニターの明るさを下げてください。
contextSentences.en: Please lower the monitor's brightness.

words.meaningMnemonic: A hungry <reading>printer</reading> eats your report and spits out a thousand paper airplanes. You chase the flying pages until the rebellious <vocabulary>printer</vocabulary> runs out of ink. プリンター is the printing device; the last vowel is held long.

contextSentences.ja: プリンターの紙がなくなった。
contextSentences.en: The printer ran out of paper.

contextSentences.ja: この写真をプリンターで印刷した。
contextSentences.en: I printed this photo with the printer.

words.meaningMnemonic: A digital <reading>file</reading> escapes its icon and slices through the screen like a metal tool. You drag the sharp <vocabulary>file</vocabulary> back into its folder before it cuts the keyboard. ファイル can be a computer file or a physical file or binder; the surrounding object or action makes the sense clear.

contextSentences.ja: 資料を一つのファイルにまとめた。
contextSentences.en: I put the materials together in one file.

contextSentences.ja: そのファイルをメールで送ってください。
contextSentences.en: Please send that file by email.

words.meaningMnemonic: A computer <reading>folder</reading> folds every document into a paper crane and stores the flock behind its icon. Opening the <vocabulary>folder</vocabulary> releases all the files into the screen. フォルダ is normally a digital folder; physical document folders may also be called ファイル.

contextSentences.ja: 写真を月ごとのフォルダに分けた。
contextSentences.en: I sorted the photos into folders by month.

contextSentences.ja: 共有フォルダに資料を入れてください。
contextSentences.en: Please put the materials in the shared folder.

words.meaningMnemonic: Your <reading>password</reading> dresses as a guard and refuses to let even you into your account. You must whisper the secret <vocabulary>password</vocabulary> to make it step aside. パスワード is the login secret; 暗証番号 is more usual for a numeric PIN.

contextSentences.ja: パスワードは他の人に教えないでください。
contextSentences.en: Please don't share your password with anyone else.

contextSentences.ja: 新しいパスワードを設定した。
contextSentences.en: I set a new password.

words.meaningMnemonic: An online <reading>account</reading> starts counting every click you make and stacks the numbers above your profile. You delete the tower but keep the registered <vocabulary>user account</vocabulary>. アカウント is an account for a service or platform; a bank account is usually 口座.

contextSentences.ja: 仕事用のアカウントでログインした。
contextSentences.en: I signed in with my work account.

contextSentences.ja: 古いアカウントを削除しました。
contextSentences.en: I deleted the old account.

words.meaningMnemonic: During a <reading>download</reading>, a cloud lowers a rope and drops thousands of files into your phone. The device sinks into the floor under the completed <vocabulary>download</vocabulary>. ダウンロード is the noun or can take する to mean downloading data to your device.

contextSentences.ja: 地図を先にダウンロードしておいた。
contextSentences.en: I downloaded the map in advance.

contextSentences.ja: このファイルは無料でダウンロードできます。
contextSentences.en: You can download this file for free.

words.readingMap: ダ・ウ・ン・ロ・ー・ド

words.meaningMnemonic: A wise sage wades into a mess of papers and stamps one sentence onto every page. The crowd calls him <reading>MESS—SAGE!</reading> when the flying papers assemble into one clear <vocabulary>message</vocabulary>. メッセージ can be a text, spoken note, or broader communication; メッセージを送る means to send one.

contextSentences.ja: 着いたらメッセージを送ってください。
contextSentences.en: Please send me a message when you arrive.

contextSentences.ja: 友達から長いメッセージが届いた。
contextSentences.en: I received a long message from a friend.

packs.title: Music, Media & Play
packs.description: High-utility entertainment and sport words for talking about what you watch, hear, and do for fun.

words.meaningMnemonic: A film editor feeds アニメーション into enormous scissors, which cut off ーション and leave <reading>アニメ</reading> dancing on the screen. The shortened characters animate themselves into a whole <vocabulary>animation</vocabulary>. In Japanese, アニメ can mean animation from any country; English often narrows anime to Japanese animation.

contextSentences.ja: 週末に新しいアニメを見始めた。
contextSentences.en: I started watching a new anime this weekend.

contextSentences.ja: このアニメは音楽もすばらしい。
contextSentences.en: The music in this anime is excellent too.

words.meaningMnemonic: A television <reading>drama</reading> becomes so dramatic that the actors climb out of the screen and continue arguing in your living room. You reach for the remote, but the <vocabulary>TV drama</vocabulary> steals it for the next episode. ドラマ commonly means a scripted television series; it can also refer more broadly to dramatic events or works.

contextSentences.ja: 毎週このドラマを楽しみにしている。
contextSentences.en: I look forward to this TV drama every week.

contextSentences.ja: 昨日のドラマは意外な終わり方だった。
contextSentences.en: Yesterday's episode of the drama had a surprising ending.

words.meaningMnemonic: The evening <reading>news</reading> anchor announces that your sofa has been elected mayor, and reporters surround it. The absurd event becomes tomorrow's front-page <vocabulary>news</vocabulary>. ニュース means reports of current events; its first vowel is held long in Japanese.

contextSentences.ja: 朝のニュースで天気を確認した。
contextSentences.en: I checked the weather on the morning news.

contextSentences.ja: そのニュースはインターネットで知った。
contextSentences.en: I first heard the news online.

words.meaningMnemonic: An old <reading>radio</reading> broadcasts your private humming to every house in town. You pull the plug, but the singing <vocabulary>radio</vocabulary> continues on battery power. ラジオ is the radio device or medium; ラジオ番組 is a radio program.

contextSentences.ja: 料理をしながらラジオを聞く。
contextSentences.en: I listen to the radio while cooking.

contextSentences.ja: ラジオで野球の試合を聞いた。
contextSentences.en: I listened to the baseball game on the radio.

words.meaningMnemonic: At a <reading>concert</reading>, the conductor points at the audience and makes everyone sing while the band listens. The crowd becomes the loudest live <vocabulary>concert</vocabulary> of the night. コンサート usually means a live musical performance, with a long サー sound in the middle.

contextSentences.ja: 来月のコンサートの券を買った。
contextSentences.en: I bought a ticket for next month's concert.

contextSentences.ja: コンサートは夜七時に始まります。
contextSentences.en: The concert starts at seven in the evening.

words.meaningMnemonic: An <reading>empty KARA + orchestra OKE</reading> leaves one terrified singer alone onstage, so recorded music rushes in to support her. She grabs the microphone and turns the empty orchestra into <vocabulary>karaoke</vocabulary>. カラオケ combines 空, empty, with オケ, a shortening of orchestra, and means singing to a backing track.

contextSentences.ja: 仕事の後でみんなとカラオケに行った。
contextSentences.en: I went to karaoke with everyone after work.

contextSentences.ja: 彼女はカラオケで昔の歌を歌った。
contextSentences.en: She sang an old song at karaoke.

words.meaningMnemonic: A pair of shoes hears <reading>dance</reading> music and drags your feet across the floor without permission. You spin until the unstoppable <vocabulary>dancing</vocabulary> shoes finally wear out. ダンス is dance as an activity or style; ダンスする means to dance.

contextSentences.ja: 妹は週に二回ダンスを習っている。
contextSentences.en: My younger sister takes dance lessons twice a week.

contextSentences.ja: 音楽に合わせてダンスをした。
contextSentences.en: We danced along with the music.

words.meaningMnemonic: A <reading>guitar</reading> strums itself so fiercely that its strings lasso everyone in the room. You calm the noisy <vocabulary>guitar</vocabulary> by playing one gentle chord. ギター is the instrument, and its final vowel is long in Japanese.

contextSentences.ja: 兄は毎晩ギターを練習する。
contextSentences.en: My older brother practices the guitar every evening.

contextSentences.ja: この曲をギターで弾いてください。
contextSentences.en: Please play this song on the guitar.

words.meaningMnemonic: A <reading>piano</reading> grows fingers and plays its own keys while the pianist takes a nap. The jealous <vocabulary>piano</vocabulary> locks its keyboard when she wakes. ピアノ is the instrument; ピアノを弾く is the usual way to say play the piano.

contextSentences.ja: 子どものころからピアノを弾いている。
contextSentences.en: I've played the piano since I was a child.

contextSentences.ja: 部屋から静かなピアノの音が聞こえる。
contextSentences.en: I can hear quiet piano music from the room.

words.meaningMnemonic: A <reading>soccer</reading> ball kicks the players and scores a goal all by itself. The referee awards the match to the ball, the true champion of <vocabulary>football</vocabulary>. サッカー is association football or soccer; the stopped consonant and long final vowel distinguish its Japanese rhythm.

contextSentences.ja: 放課後に公園でサッカーをした。
contextSentences.en: We played soccer in the park after school.

contextSentences.ja: 父とサッカーの試合を見に行く。
contextSentences.en: I'm going to watch a soccer match with my father.

packs.title: Shopping Smart
packs.description: Useful retail and payment language for finding the right item, paying, and keeping track of a purchase.

words.meaningMnemonic: A <reading>shopping</reading> cart grabs your wallet and races from store to store buying everything it sees. You stop its wild <vocabulary>shopping</vocabulary> spree only when the card declines. ショッピング means the activity of shopping, often for pleasure; 買い物 is the broader everyday native word.

contextSentences.ja: 休日に家族とショッピングに出かけた。
contextSentences.en: I went shopping with my family on my day off.

contextSentences.ja: 最近は家でオンラインショッピングをすることが多い。
contextSentences.en: Lately, I often shop online from home.

words.readingMap: ショ・ッ・ピ・ン・グ

words.meaningMnemonic: A red <reading>SALE</reading> sign grows sails and blows discounted products out of the shop. You catch a half-price coat as the <vocabulary>sale</vocabulary> storm passes. セール is a promotional sale or discount event, with the first vowel held long.

contextSentences.ja: この店は明日からセールです。
contextSentences.en: This shop's sale starts tomorrow.

contextSentences.ja: セールでコートを安く買った。
contextSentences.en: I bought a coat at a discount during the sale.

words.meaningMnemonic: A flashing <reading>BARGAIN</reading> sign wrestles every price tag to the floor and pins it at half price. Shoppers rush into the resulting <vocabulary>bargain sale</vocabulary>. バーゲン usually means a bargain-sale event in Japanese, not simply one good deal or a verb for negotiating.

contextSentences.ja: 夏のバーゲンは来週始まる。
contextSentences.en: The summer bargain sale starts next week.

contextSentences.ja: バーゲンで靴を二足買った。
contextSentences.en: I bought two pairs of shoes at the bargain sale.

words.meaningMnemonic: A <reading>coupon</reading> leaps from your phone and bites ten percent off the price tag. The cashier catches the paper teeth and accepts the <vocabulary>voucher</vocabulary>. クーポン is a coupon or discount code, and its first vowel is held long.

contextSentences.ja: 会計の前にクーポンを見せた。
contextSentences.en: I showed the coupon before paying.

contextSentences.ja: このクーポンは今月末まで使えます。
contextSentences.en: This coupon can be used until the end of this month.

words.meaningMnemonic: Each <reading>point</reading> on your loyalty card turns into a tiny gold coin and marches toward a prize. After enough purchases, the army of <vocabulary>reward points</vocabulary> carries the prize home. ポイント often means loyalty points here; it can also mean a key point, score, or other kind of point in different contexts.

contextSentences.ja: 買い物でポイントが百たまった。
contextSentences.en: I earned one hundred points from the purchase.

contextSentences.ja: 今日はポイントを使って払います。
contextSentences.en: I'll pay using points today.

words.meaningMnemonic: A <reading>credit card</reading> takes credit for everything you buy and signs its own name on the receipt. You lock the boastful <vocabulary>credit card</vocabulary> in your wallet before it shops alone. クレジットカード is the full term; カード alone can mean many different kinds of card.

contextSentences.ja: クレジットカードで払えますか。
contextSentences.en: Can I pay by credit card?

contextSentences.ja: クレジットカードの明細を確認した。
contextSentences.en: I checked my credit card statement.

words.readingMap: ク・レ・ジ・ッ・ト・カ・ー・ド

words.meaningMnemonic: At a <reading>cashless</reading> shop, every coin that enters turns invisible and jumps back into your pocket. Only a phone tap opens the register, making the entire payment <vocabulary>cashless</vocabulary>. キャッシュレス describes payments or businesses that do not use physical cash; it does not mean free of charge.

contextSentences.ja: この店はキャッシュレス決済だけです。
contextSentences.en: This shop accepts only cashless payments.

contextSentences.ja: 旅行中はキャッシュレスで支払うことが多い。
contextSentences.en: I often use cashless payment while traveling.

words.readingMap: キャ・ッ・シュ・レ・ス

words.meaningMnemonic: A magical <reading>staff</reading> splits into ten workers who stock shelves, greet customers, and clean the floor. When the work is done, the whole <vocabulary>staff</vocabulary> merges back into one stick. スタッフ can mean the staff collectively or an individual staff member; スタッフの人 makes the individual explicit.

contextSentences.ja: 分からないことをスタッフに聞いた。
contextSentences.en: I asked a staff member about something I didn't understand.

contextSentences.ja: 店のスタッフが丁寧に説明してくれた。
contextSentences.en: The store staff explained it politely.

words.meaningMnemonic: A shirt's <reading>size</reading> label swells from S to enormous, and the shirt grows until it fills the store. The tailor cuts the <vocabulary>size</vocabulary> back down before anyone is buried. サイズ means dimensions or a labeled size category; サイズが合う means the size fits.

contextSentences.ja: もう一つ大きいサイズはありますか。
contextSentences.en: Do you have this in one size larger?

contextSentences.ja: 靴のサイズを店員に伝えた。
contextSentences.en: I told the clerk my shoe size.

words.meaningMnemonic: A glowing <reading>brand</reading> stamp jumps from product to product, marking every box with the same maker's name. Customers follow the mark to identify the <vocabulary>brand</vocabulary>. ブランド means a commercial brand or designer label, not the hot iron or the act of branding.

contextSentences.ja: このブランドは丈夫なかばんで有名だ。
contextSentences.en: This brand is famous for durable bags.

contextSentences.ja: ブランドより使いやすさを重視します。
contextSentences.en: I value ease of use more than the brand.

words.meaningMnemonic: A wrapped <reading>present</reading> punches a calendar marked present time and knocks it off the wall. The box cares only about being opened as a <vocabulary>gift</vocabulary>. プレゼント means a gift, not the current moment; プレゼントする means to give one.

contextSentences.ja: 友達の誕生日に本をプレゼントした。
contextSentences.en: I gave my friend a book for their birthday.

contextSentences.ja: この箱はプレゼントです。
contextSentences.en: This box is a gift.

words.meaningMnemonic: A long <reading>receipt</reading> snakes out of the register, wraps around your purchases, and refuses to let go. You show the printed <vocabulary>receipt</vocabulary> to prove every item was paid for. レシート is the itemized shop receipt; 領収書 is the more formal receipt often requested for accounting.

contextSentences.ja: レシートは袋に入れてください。
contextSentences.en: Please put the receipt in the bag.

contextSentences.ja: 返品にはレシートが必要です。
contextSentences.en: A receipt is required for returns.
